The prevalence of misinformation poses a substantial threat to individuals' daily lives, necessitating the deployment of effective remedial approaches. One promising strategy is psychological inoculation, which pre-emptively immunizes individuals against misinformation attacks. However, uncertainties remain regarding the extent to which psychological inoculation effectively enhances the capacity to differentiate between misinformation and real information.

To reduce the potential risk of misinformation about digital health, this study aims to examine the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in countering misinformation with a focus on several factors, including misinformation credibility assessment, real information credibility assessment, credibility discernment, misinformation sharing intention, real information sharing intention, and sharing discernment.

Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines, we conducted a meta-analysis by searching 4 databases (Web of Science, APA PsycINFO, Proquest, and PubMed) for empirical studies based on inoculation theory and outcome measure–related misinformation published in the English language. Moderator analyses were used to examine the differences in intervention strategy, intervention type, theme, measurement time, team, and intervention design.

Based on 42 independent studies with 42,530 subjects, we found that psychological inoculation effectively reduces misinformation credibility assessment (

=–0.36, 95% CI –0.50 to –0.23;

<.001) and improves real information credibility assessment (

=0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.33;

=.005) and real information sharing intention (

=0.09, 95% CI 0.03-0.16;

=.003). However, psychological inoculation does not significantly influence misinformation sharing intention (

=–0.35, 95% CI –0.79 to 0.09;

=.12). Additionally, we find that psychological inoculation effectively enhances credibility discernment (

=0.20, 95% CI 0.13-0.28;

<.001) and sharing discernment (

=0.18, 95% CI 0.12-0.24;

<.001). Regarding health misinformation, psychological inoculation effectively decreases misinformation credibility assessment and misinformation sharing intention. The results of the moderator analyses showed that content-based, passive inoculation was more effective in increasing credibility and sharing intention. The theme of

climate change

demonstrates a stronger effect on real information credibility. Comparing intervention types showed that pre-post interventions are more effective for misinformation credibility assessment, while post-only interventions are better for credibility discernment.

Conclusions

This study indicated that psychological inoculation enhanced individuals' ability to discern real information from misinformation and share real information. Incorporating psychological inoculation to cultivate an informed public is crucial for societal resilience against misinformation threats in an age of information proliferation. As a scalable and cost-effective intervention strategy, institutions can apply psychological inoculation to mitigate potential misinformation crises.

psychological inoculation, misinformation, discernment, sharing, meta-analysis

Introduction

Misinformation has become a global problem that threatens people's daily lives. For example, climate change misinformation confuses the public's perception of anthropogenic climate change \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref1

\], and COVID-19 misinformation prevents people from finding effective treatment strategies \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref2

\]. In light of the escalating challenges posed by misinformation, it becomes increasingly evident that honing individuals' discernment skills is paramount to safeguarding public health and overall well-being.

Misinformation refers to information that is false, but not created with the intention of causing harm \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref3

\]. Misinformation is usually measured using self-reports.

In this field of study, researchers present a series of social media posts or news statements containing true or false information to subjects \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref4

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref5

\], after which a binary or Likert scale is used to allow the subjects to assess the information's credibility and their willingness to share it. However, these methods are somewhat limited. For example, the effect of the intervention may simultaneously reduce the credibility of all the information \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref6

\]. Researchers are currently more interested in the concept of “discernment,” which assesses an individual's ability to discriminate misinformation from real information by calculating the difference between real information and misinformation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref7

Psychological Inoculation

Studies have provided strategies against misinformation, such as improving social media and filtering algorithms \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref8

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref9

\]. Research has attempted to combat misinformation using a “prebunking” method called psychological inoculation, which confers potential resistance to misinformation before encountering it. Psychological inoculation suggests that the idea of injecting a weakened dose of a virus to activate antibodies can be applied in the context of information processing. It works in 2 ways \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref10

\]: motivational threat (the desire to defend against manipulation attacks) and refutational pre-emption (pre-exposure to a weakened example of the attack).

Traditional psychological inoculation research has focused on health behavior promotion, but it is now more focused on misinformation issues \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref11

\]. For example, the Bad News game designed by Roozenbeek and van der Linden \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref5

\] teaches players about 6 common misinformation strategies by putting them in the role of the creator of misinformation. The result shows that inoculation reduces the perceived reliability and persuasiveness of misinformation. The method has been recognized by the European Commission as the most sustainable means of combating misinformation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref12

\] and has achieved equally significant results in cross-cultural research. Piltch-Loeb et al \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref13

\] promoted resistance to COVID-19 vaccine misinformation with a video inoculation. Results found that the inoculated individuals showed greater resistance to misinformation than the uninoculated individuals. Agley et al \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref14

\] presented an intervention infographic to prevent COVID-19 misinformation.

Recently, there has been some debate about the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in response to misinformation. Some researchers argue that psychological inoculation reduces the belief in all information and that the ability to effectively discriminate between real and false information is not improved \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref15

\]. Additionally, the field has moved from “content-based” to “technology-based” immunization, and the application of active (vs passive) inoculations \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref10

\]. However, the effectiveness of these strategies requires further investigation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref16

Based on these concerns, this study conducted a meta-analysis to investigate the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in combating misinformation, focusing on the influence of misinformation credibility assessment, real information credibility assessment, credibility discernment, misinformation sharing intention, real information sharing intention, and sharing discernment. In addition, we further investigated the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in response to health misinformation. During COVID-19, the increasing risk of misinformation, such as vaccination hesitancy driven by misinformation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref17

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref18

\], created a new challenge for general public health in the online setting. Comprehending the efficacy of psychological inoculation as a response to misinformation can establish a reliable foundation for subsequent policy implementation.

Potential Moderators

Many study characteristics influence the intervention effect \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref19

\]. We examined the following moderators: intervention strategy, intervention type, theme, measurement time, team, and intervention design.

Intervention strategies and types may have an impact on the effects of psychological inoculation. For the intervention strategies, content-based inoculation focuses on the content of the information, and technology-based inoculation focuses on the technology behind the information \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref10

\]. Whether technology-based inoculation can achieve a similar effect to content-based inoculation needs to be further tested. For the intervention type, passive inoculation requires that participants be asked to read the rebuttals provided in the inoculation information without actively engaging in generating their own responses \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref20

\]. Active inoculation requires participants to generate their own rebuttals in response to the rebuttal information provided. The cognitive processes involved in active inoculation, which involves “internal” rebuttals, are more effective than passive inoculation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref21

\]. In this study, graphics and courses were classified as passive inoculation, while videos and games were classified as active inoculation because they were more likely to prompt people to generate responses.

Misinformation interventions commonly engage with different themes, with current major themes including climate change, policy, and health \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref1

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref14

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref22

\]; whether these interventions are effective for additional issues also needs to be investigated.

The durability of misinformation is an important indicator of intervention effectiveness and when additional intervention is needed \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref23

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref24

\]. Therefore, the difference in measurement time of psychological inoculation needs to be clarified. Based on the existing study, we divided the measurement time into “immediately,” “1-week follow-up,” and “2 weeks or more” \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref25

The team of authors may also influence the effectiveness of psychological inoculation. Van der Linden's team \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref1

\] introduced psychological inoculation into the misinformation issue and has conducted many related studies with his collaborators \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref24

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref26

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref28

\]. We used van der Linden's team and other researchers as a moderator to examine the reliability of the psychological inoculation effect.

Despite the existence of a control group, different intervention designs may still affect intervention results. For example, the intervention effects may be different in the post-only test condition than in the pre-post test condition \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref27

\]. We distinguished between these 2 intervention designs to validate the inoculation effect.

Literature Retrieval

This meta-analysis followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis) guidelines (see

Multimedia Appendix 1

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#app1

) for identifying studies \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref29

\]. A literature search was conducted in electronic databases including Web of Science, APA PsycINFO, Proquest, and PubMed. The following 2 search strings were combined using Boolean search terms in titles, abstracts, and keywords: (“Inoculating” OR “Inoculation”) AND (“misinformation” OR “disinformation” OR “conspiracy theor\*” OR “fake news” OR “rumor” OR “false information”). Specific search strategies for different databases can be accessed in

Multimedia Appendix 2

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#app2

. The initial database search was conducted until April 2023. A summary of the study flow is shown in

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#figure1

Inclusion Criteria

The inclusion and exclusion criteria of this study are shown in

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#box1

Inclusion and exclusion criteria.

Inclusion criteria

Studies covering people who may have been exposed to misinformation

Studies based on inoculation theory that included a control group for comparison

Studies that included a placebo, no inoculation intervention, or no intervention as a control

Studies with the outcomes of misinformation credibility assessment, real information credibility assessment, credibility discernment, misinformation sharing intention, real information sharing intention, and sharing discernment

Studies measuring assessment of information, changes in attitudes, or behavioral intentions

Studies that included randomized controlled trials

Empirical, peer-reviewed studies

Studies providing effect size or data to enable the calculation of effect sizes

Studies written in English

Exclusion criteria

Studies including children younger than 6 years; these require adult supervision according to European Union regulations

Studies not based on inoculation theory

Studies not including a control group

Studies not related to credibility assessment and sharing intention for real information or misinformation

Studies including non–randomized controlled trials

Reviews and nonempirical studies

Studies not providing enough data to enable the calculation of effect sizes

Studies not written in English

Data Extraction

Relevant data were extracted from the selected studies, including study information (first author and year of publication), sample size, study country, sample age, misinformation theme, intervention type (active vs passive), intervention strategy (content-based vs technology-based), measurement, measurement time, team (van der Linden's team vs others), intervention design (post only and pre-post), and outcome (misinformation credibility assessment, real information credibility assessment, credibility discernment, misinformation sharing intention, real information sharing intention, and sharing discernment).

Quality Assessment

The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool (RoB 2.0) was used to assess intervention studies \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref30

\]. Funnel plots, the Egger regression test \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref31

\], the precision-effect test (PET), and the precision-effect estimate with SE (PET-PEESE) were used to examine publication bias in intervention studies \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref32

\], and the Duval and Tweedie \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref33

\] trim-and-fill method was used to adjust for publication bias. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed to ensure that no single study significantly influenced the results. Two independent coders assessed the quality of the studies according to the criteria of these tools. There were no significant differences between the 2 coders.

Data Analysis

In this study, the effect size is calculated using the Cohen

, which refers to a standardized difference in means standardized by the change in SD. The Cohen

was calculated using R (R Core Team). For each study, means, SDs, and sample size were extracted. If the study did not report statistics, the Cohen

was calculated using

values. The Cohen

distinguishment criteria were as follows: 0.2 for a small effect size, 0.5 for a medium effect size, and 0.8 for a large effect size \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref34

\]. A negative value indicated lower credibility assessment and sharing intention for misinformation and real information compared to the control conditions. A positive value indicated a higher discernment ability for credibility and sharing compared to the control conditions. The

statistic and

statistic were used to estimate heterogeneity and a random effect model was used to combine effect sizes. Moderator analyses were used to examine potential moderators that might influence intervention effects \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref35

\]. All analyses were conducted using the

(version 6.2-1),

(version 0.0.9000), and

(version 3.8-1) R packages \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref36

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref38

value <.05 was considered statistically significant.

A total of 29 articles that included 42 independent studies with a total sample size of 42,530 were included in this meta-analysis. Specific information on all included studies can be accessed in

. Research on psychological inoculation against misinformation was mainly published from 2017 to 2023, with most studies conducted with immediate measurement (k=35). Psychological Inoculation Against Health Misinformation

Due to the public concern about health misinformation after COVID-19, we further analyzed the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in combating health misinformation. We included studies that focused only on the health theme of

misinformation

(studies with multiple themes were not included). A total of 15 independent studies with 6732 subjects were included. Studies were published from 2021 to 2023, implying that psychological inoculation responded to health misinformation that emerged with the outbreak of COVID-19. The mean age of the participants was 36 years. The main study countries were the United States (k=10) and China (k=3), and the studies were conducted mainly with graphics (k=13).

In combined studies of health misinformation, we found that psychological inoculation significantly reduced the health misinformation credibility assessment (

=0.28, 95% CI –0.41 to –0.15;

<.001; k=9) and sharing intention (

=–0.19, 95% CI –0.30 to –0.08;

=.001; k=4). However, psychological inoculation did not have an effect on health real information credibility assessment (

=0.05, 95% CI–0.15 to 0.25;

=.61; k=7), sharing intention (

=0.15, 95% CI –0.01 to 0.30;

=.07; k=5), credibility discernment (

=0.06, 95% CI –0.06 to 0.18;

=.34; k=2), or sharing discernment (

=0.10, 95% CI –0.02 to 0.22;

=.09; k=2).

Principal Findings

In this study, we conducted a meta-analysis to examine the effectiveness of psychological inoculation against misinformation. Based on 42 independent studies, we found that psychological inoculation was effective in reducing misinformation credibility assessment and improving real information credibility assessment as well as real information sharing intention. However, psychological inoculation did not effectively influence misinformation sharing intention. For discernment, we found that psychological inoculation was effective in improving ability for credibility discernment and sharing discernment.

The Effectiveness of Psychological Inoculation Against Misinformation

First, psychological inoculation was effective in reducing misinformation credibility assessment (

=–0.36) and improving real information credibility assessment (

=0.20) and real information sharing intention (

=0.09). This is consistent with existing research that psychological inoculation increases people's immunity to misinformation and makes them less likely to believe the misinformation they subsequently encounter \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref5

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref57

\]. Second, psychological inoculation did not effectively influence misinformation sharing intention (

=.12). This indicates that the effectiveness of psychological inoculation in reducing the dissemination of misinformation is moderate. A possible reason is that individuals sharing misinformation are influenced by other factors \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref58

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref59

\]. Last, psychological inoculation was effective in improving abilities for credibility discernment (

=0.20) and sharing discernment (

=0.18). Contrary to the opinion that psychological inoculation reduces the credibility of all information \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref6

\], psychological inoculation improves individuals' ability to distinguish between real information and misinformation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref7

\]. This extends psychological inoculation's practical implications. These results suggest that psychological inoculation is an effective method for helping the public cope with the misinformation they receive.

The Effectiveness of Psychological Inoculation Against Health Misinformation

Psychological inoculation also effectively decreased misinformation credibility assessment (

=0.28) and sharing intention (

=–0.19). This is consistent with previous studies \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref13

\], indicating the efficacy of psychological inoculation in helping the public cope with the risk of health misinformation. However, psychological inoculation did not influence real information credibility assessment and sharing intention or credibility discernment and sharing discernment. This demonstrates that psychological inoculation was insufficient to boost public trust in real information on health.

Moderator Analysis

First, different intervention types and intervention strategies did not affect credibility and sharing intention for misinformation, but content-based and passive inoculation were more effective in increasing credibility and sharing intention for real information. A possible reason is that interventions place more focus on reliable statements themselves when performing the inoculation, which leads to better results. Second, the theme of

climate change

had a better effect on real information credibility after inoculation, which implies the great potential of psychological inoculation to respond to the climate change crisis. Third, there was no significant difference in the measurement time, which implies that psychological inoculation may have good durability \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref24

\]. Fourth, van der Linden's team did not differ significantly from other researchers, implying that different research teams arrived at similar results, increasing the reliability and generalizability of the results. Finally, the intervention design influenced the intervention effect for misinformation credibility assessment and credibility discernment. Pre-post interventions were more effective than post-only interventions for misinformation credibility assessment. However, the post-only interventions were better than pre-post interventions for credibility discernment. Intervention effects may be magnified because the post-only condition does not assess preintervention status. Similarly, in the pre-post condition studies, there may have been a practice effect among subjects who answered the same questions and thus achieved better results \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref27

Limitations

Current research on countering misinformation through psychological inoculation has some limitations, and future research needs to expand its scope. First, most of the current studies did not examine decay trends and only assessed the durability of intervention effects at separate time points. Future studies could assess effects at more time points to clarify when the best effects are reached after intervention and when they decay rapidly. Second, most of the studies were conducted in Western countries through online interventions. There is a lack of testing of the effects in a standardized laboratory setting, and cultural representativeness has also not been considered. Future studies should examine the effects of psychological inoculation in standard laboratory conditions and test them in Eastern countries. Finally, most current studies have been conducted with adults and representative populations, although older adults and adolescents tend to be more susceptible to misinformation \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref60

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref61

\]. Future studies need to focus on these susceptible groups.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that psychological inoculation is an effective approach against misinformation. It effectively strengthens individuals' discernment abilities, enabling them to distinguish between genuine and false information. Furthermore, when applied to health misinformation, psychological inoculation shows promise in diminishing credibility assessment and sharing intention for health-related falsehoods, contributing to safeguarding public health. These findings have profound implications for public health and digital well-being. Psychological inoculation can be easily scaled to a broad population at a low cost, and institutions can apply it to mitigate potential misinformation crises \[

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10498317/#ref7

\]. Incorporating psychological inoculation strategies into public health initiatives and educational programs can empower individuals to make well-informed decisions in an era characterized by information proliferation. Cultivating a discerning and well-informed public is crucial to building societal resilience against the pervasive threats posed by misinformation.

BNPA Lifetime Achievement Award   Psychological inoculation against misinformation

Sander van der Linden

Professor of Social Psychology in Society, University of Cambridge, UK

Sander van der Linden is Professor of Social Psychology in Society in the Department of Psychology at the University of Cambridge and Director of the Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab. Before coming to Cambridge, he held posts at Princeton and Yale University. His research interests center around the psychology of human judgment and decision-making. In particular, he is interested in the social influence and persuasion process and how people are influenced by (mis)information and gain resistance to persuasion through psychological inoculation. He is also interested in the study of fake news, media effects, social networks, and belief systems (e.g., conspiracy theories), as well as the emergence of social norms, polarization, reasoning about evidence, and public understanding of risk and uncertainty. His research spans from social psychology to cognitive science using a variety of techniques, from virtual reality to survey and lab studies to computational social science and large-scale (online) interventions.

His forthcoming book FOOLPROOF: Why Misinformation Infects Our Brains, and How to Build Immunity (WW Norton/HarperCollins) is to be published later this month. He has published around 150 papers and is ranked among the top 1% of all social scientists worldwide (Clarivate ISI Highly Cited Researcher) and among the top 2% across all scientific fields (Ioannidis, Boyack, & Baas, 2020).

Much like a viral contagion, misinformation can spread rapidly from one mind to another. Moreover, once lodged in memory, misinformation is difficult to correct. Inoculation theory therefore offers a natural basis for developing a psychological ‘vaccine’ against the spread of fake news and misinformation. Specifically, in a series of randomized lab and field studies, I’ll show that it is possible to pre-emptively ‘immunize’ people against disinformation about a wide range of topics by pre-exposing them to severely weakened doses of the techniques that underlie its production. This process of ‘prebunking’ helps people cultivate cognitive antibodies in a simulated social media environment. During the talk, I’ll showcase several real-world interventions we developed and empirically evaluated in 20 languages—with governments and social media companies—to help citizens around the world recognize and resist unwanted attempts to influence and mislead.

#### Background:

The promise of precision medicine could be stymied if people do not accept the legitimacy of personalized risk information. We tested four explanations for skepticism of personalized diabetes risk information.

We recruited participants (

=48.6 \[SD=9.8\], 85.1% women, 59.0% non-Hispanic white) from community locations (e.g., barbershops, churches) for a risk communication intervention. Participants received personalized information about their risk of developing diabetes and heart disease, stroke, colon cancer, and/or breast cancer (women). Then they completed survey items. We combined two items (recalled risk, perceived risk) to create a trichotomous risk skepticism variable (acceptance, overestimation, underestimation). Additional items assessed possible explanations for risk skepticism: (1)

information evaluation skills

(education, graph literacy, numeracy); (2)

motivated reasoning

(negative affect toward the information, spontaneous self-affirmation, information avoidance); (3)

Bayesian updating

(surprise); and (4)

personal relevance

(racial/ethnic identity). We used multinomial logistic regression for data analysis.

18% of participants believed that their diabetes risk was lower than the information provided, 40% believed their risk was higher, and 42% accepted the information.

Information evaluation skills

were not supported as a risk skepticism explanation.

Motivated reasoning

received some support; higher diabetes risk and more negative affect toward the information were associated with risk underestimation, but spontaneous self-affirmation and information avoidance were not moderators. For

Bayesian updating

, more surprise was associated with overestimation. For

personal relevance

, belonging to a marginalized racial/ethnic group was associated with underestimation.

#### Conclusion:

There are likely multiple cognitive, affective, and motivational explanations for risk skepticism. Understanding these explanations and developing interventions that address them will increase the effectiveness of precision medicine and facilitate its widespread implementation.

Risk perception, Decision making, Motivated reasoning, Health communication, Precision medicine

Introduction

Risk prediction models are a cornerstone of precision medicine. They can use demographic and health history information to estimate how likely an individual is to develop a disease, respond to a particular medical therapeutic, or survive an illness (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R1

). Many models have been translated into interactive risk assessment tools (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R2

), under the assumption that informing people of their personalized risk could motivate engagement in health protective behaviors (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R3

). Yet, although personalized disease risk information can increase the accuracy of people's risk perceptions (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R4

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R5

), its effects on physical activity, alcohol consumption, and smoking behavior are limited (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R6

One possible reason for the limited effectiveness of personalized risk communication is risk skepticism. In this paper, we define risk skepticism as occurring when individuals report believing that the personalized risk information provided by a formal risk assessment tool is incorrect (i.e., they express doubt about the validity or reliability of the risk information (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R8

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#FN5

For example, approximately 20% to 25% of women who received personalized breast cancer risk estimates reported that they thought that their actual risk was different from the estimate that they were provided (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R4

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R9

). Risk skepticism has also been reported for personalized risk estimates for Alzheimer's Disease (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R10

), colon cancer (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

), breast cancer (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R11

), heart disease (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R8

), heart attack (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R12

), lung cancer (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R13

), and prostate cancer (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R14

Despite evidence that some people are skeptical of personalized risk information, limited research has explored explanations for its occurrence. In addition, risk rejection can occur in either direction—that is, people can report that they think that their risk is higher or lower than they are told (i.e., they overestimate or underestimate their risk, respectively; (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

) ). Yet, no studies of risk skepticism have described what predicts overestimation or underestimation. Understanding what leads to risk skepticism, in which direction people are skeptical of their risk information, and, critically, the consequences of risk in both directions—will inform development and implementation of communication strategies and other interventions that maximize acceptance of personalized risk information and thereby achieve the goal of precision medicine to improve public health. This study represents the first of several necessary steps to achieve this goal.

Explanations for Risk Skepticism

We identified four likely explanations for risk skepticism (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R15

). First, risk skepticism could result from people misunderstanding the risk information they are provided (i.e.,

information evaluation skills

). Specifically, people with less ability to understand and use the information, such as those with limited numeracy, will be more likely to be skeptical of personalized risk information (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R16

Second, learning one's disease risk can be affectively aversive, and risk skepticism could help manage negative affect (i.e.,

motivated reasoning

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R17

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R19

)). For example, a personalized risk estimate might be affectively aversive if it confers high cancer risk or requires engaging in an undesired behavior (e.g., unpleasant screening) (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R20

). Thus, higher risk estimates would be threatening, elicit negative affect, and would be associated with believing that one's risk is lower than the risk estimate (see also research related to the optimistic bias (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R21

) and information suppression (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

) ). In addition, we expect the motivated reasoning tendency to be attenuated among people who engage in cognitive activities shown to reduce motivated reasoning. For example, people who tend to reflect on their personal values when threatened (i.e.,

spontaneous self-affirmation

) display more openness to potentially threatening health information (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R23

). In contrast, people who report greater general tendencies to avoid health information (i.e.,

information avoidance tendencies

) may show a stronger relationship between higher risk estimates and greater risk underestimation, as information avoidance may be a strategy to reduce feelings of threat brought about by health information (see also research related to attention avoidance (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

Third, people may be more likely to be skeptical of their risk estimate when it violates their prior knowledge and beliefs about their risk (i.e.,

Bayesian reasoning

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R24

)). According to this explanation, the risk estimate is not threatening

. Instead, a surprisingly high

low risk estimate draws more scrutiny (or counterargumentation (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

) ) than an expected risk estimate, increasing the likelihood of skepticism. Several studies have shown that people's risk estimates are influenced by their preexisting cognitions and beliefs about their risk (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R9

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R13

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R25

), and the more an individual's expectancies differ from their estimated risk (and therefore the more surprising the results), the more likely they are to be skeptical. For example, (Weinstein et al., 2004) reported that, although many participants adjusted their colon cancer risk estimates to become more consistent with the estimate provided by a colon cancer risk calculator, participants who initially believed that their risk was higher adjusted their risk to a lesser extent.

Fourth, some people may discount health risk information because they believe that the information is based on data from people who are unlike them or who do not represent them (i.e.,

personal relevance

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R26

)). Many factors influence people's perception of personal relevance (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R27

). Particularly relevant for risk assessment tools are the perspectives of people from racial and ethnic groups in the U.S. who are intentionally, systematically, and structurally excluded from or underrepresented in research that establishes standards of care, who may perceive risk information as less personally relevant (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R28

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R29

). For example, a Black woman might reasonably conclude that a personalized risk estimate is less valid for her than it is for a white woman (even though there have been efforts to make breast cancer risk estimates more valid for Black women) (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R30

). Indeed, there is controversy about the validity of algorithms for underrepresented populations (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R31

), in part because such algorithms seldom account for the social and structural factors that place people from excluded populations at particularly greater risk. Hence, people's reasonable concerns about the relevance of the populations used to create risk prediction models to themselves could influence whether they accept their risk information (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R26

). (Note that asserting lack of personal relevance can also be used as a motivated reasoning-based counterarguing strategy (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

). However, in this particular case of socio-demographic groups that have been underrepresented in medical research, it could be a reasonable explanation for risk skepticism.)

Objectives and Hypotheses

We investigated reasons people might be skeptical of personalized Type 2 diabetes risk information and in which direction they are skeptical (i.e., they

their risk, believing their actual risk is comparable to the information they were told; they

underestimate

their risk, believing their actual risk is lower than they were told; and they

overestimate

their risk, believing their actual risk is higher than they were told). We chose to study risk skepticism in the context of Type 2 diabetes because diabetes is a severe and common disease (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R32

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R33

), is modifiable through health behavior change (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R34

), and has risk assessment tools that are understudied. Although there are several Type 2 diabetes risk assessment tools available online (e.g., (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R2

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R35

)), there is also a dearth of research describing people's responses to being provided personalized estimates about their risk of developing Type 2 diabetes. The only exception (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R36

) reported that providing personalized pre-diabetes risk estimates prompted participants' risk perceptions to become more accurate, but only among individuals who initially underestimated their risk. Although the authors attributed these findings to motivated reasoning, that study was not designed to formally test motivated reasoning or other psychological phenomena as possible explanations for its results.

This study describes a secondary analysis of data from a two-part risk communication and behavior change intervention administered by smartphone (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R37

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R38

). We preregistered our hypotheses and planned analyses for the present study prior to examining the data (see

https://osf.io/9ab5f/?view\_only=8cb439052ee34473aa9378652ac89c72

https://osf.io/9ab5f/?view\_only=8cb439052ee34473aa9378652ac89c72

Information evaluation skills: Compared to people with more formal education, higher numeracy, and higher graph literacy, people with (a) less formal education, (b) lower numeracy, and (c) lower graph literacy will be more likely to either overestimate (vs. accept) their personalized risk information or to underestimate (vs. accept) their risk information.

2a. Motivated reasoning: Compared to people who are told that they have lower risk of developing diabetes, people who are told that they have a higher risk will be more likely to underestimate (vs. accept) their risk or to underestimate (vs. overestimate) their risk; however, the relationship between diabetes risk information and risk underestimation will be attenuated by effect modifiers among people who (i) spontaneously self-affirm or (ii) report more health information avoidance.

2b. Motivated reasoning: Compared to people with less negative affective attitudes toward exercise and less negative affect toward the risk information they were provided, people with (i) more negative affective attitudes toward exercise or (ii) more negative affect towards the risk information will be more likely to underestimate (vs. accept) their risk or to underestimate (vs. overestimate) their risk.

Bayesian updating: Compared to people who are less surprised about the diabetes risk information they are provided, people who are more surprised will be more likely to overestimate (vs. accept) or underestimate (vs. accept) their risk.

Personal relevance based on race and ethnicity: Compared to non-Hispanic white participants, participants from racial or ethnic groups that have been excluded from research in the U.S. (i.e., Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian) will be more likely to overestimate (vs. accept) or underestimate (vs. accept) their risk.

Exploratory research question: Women and people who are older and who have more comorbidities have greater contact with the healthcare system. Therefore, they may have different perspectives on health information than men and people with fewer comorbidities. However, no hypotheses were specified a priori about the direction of effects. Therefore, we examined how age, gender, and number of comorbidities were associated with risk skepticism.

Detailed information about all aspects of the methods for the parent risk communication and behavior change intervention can be found in (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R37

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R38

). All study materials for the entire intervention, including recruitment materials, stimuli, surveys, datasets, data codebooks, and statistical code can be found at:

https://osf.io/jnwhq/

https://osf.io/jnwhq/

. Datasets, codebooks, and statistical code specific to this study are at:

https://osf.io/j82f3/

https://osf.io/j82f3/

. All procedures and methods were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Washington University in St. Louis. The description below includes only the information needed to test the hypotheses above.

Participants

Individuals were eligible for the parent intervention if they were age 30–64, spoke English, and engaged in less than 150 minutes or more of aerobic physical activity per week. We also excluded people who had two or more of the following health conditions: heart disease, stroke, diabetes, or a history of cancer (except non-melanoma skin cancer). Part of the parent study relied on text messaging, so we also excluded individuals who had not texted at least twice in the last month and/or who shared a cell phone.

From July 2017 to August 2018, we engaged in recruitment activities with the goal of recruiting 505 participants, 50% (+/− 5%) with no college experience and 50% (+/− 5%) from racial and ethnic groups that have been underrepresented in research (i.e., Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian). Recruitment strategies included in-person outreach (e.g., beauty schools, churches, job fairs), paid social media and online advertisements, newspaper advertisements, two research participant registry databases, a University listserv, and word of mouth.

We based sample size calculations on the requirements of the parent intervention. The secondary analyses presented here included 356 participants. For detailed information about the participant inclusion and exclusion process, see

Online Supplemental Materials Section A

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

Procedure and Stimuli for the Parent Intervention

During an in-person appointment with a research assistant, participants independently used a smartphone to complete a risk assessment that included items assessing demographic and health history characteristics, family history, and engagement in health behaviors (median completion time=4.4 minutes). With this information, we calculated: (a) personalized 10-year absolute risk estimates for diabetes, heart disease, stroke, colon cancer, and, for women, breast cancer, and (b) personalized estimates for those same diseases, given 3 hours of physical activity weekly (hereafter

risk reduction information

Participants were then randomly assigned to view their risk and risk reduction information as a bulleted list, simple table, or risk ladder (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R38

). We provided risk and risk reduction information using category labels (i.e., very low, low, medium, high, very high; see

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#F1

. For an explanation of why we did not include numerical estimates, see (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R38

)). We did not provide participants with information about diseases for which they reported an existing personal diagnosis. After viewing their risk and risk reduction information, participants returned the phone to the research assistant and completed a post-intervention survey (which did not show their personal diabetes risk information but did include the items necessary for the analyses reported here) using paper and pen. Then they completed the second part of the intervention; it is not related to these analyses and will not be discussed further (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R37

Open in a new tab

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/figure/F1/

Three risk communication formats: bulleted list, simple table, and risk ladder (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R9

All measures below were assessed in the post-intervention survey, unless otherwise noted. We obtained all survey measures from prior research. Guided by cognitive interviews, we modified items to reduce the literacy requirements and to ensure the items were relevant for our participants and study. The complete surveys are at

https://osf.io/jnwhq/?view\_only=542fce8894e248c695e3e5d03fdf3a30

Risk Skepticism

Consistent with (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

), we used two items to create the diabetes risk skepticism outcome variable: diabetes risk recall (

“According to the \[risk assessment tool\], what are your chances of getting diabetes if you DO NOT exercise?”

) and diabetes risk belief (

“You may or may not agree with what the \[risk assessment tool\] said. What do YOU believe are your chances of getting diabetes if you DO NOT exercise?

”). Response options for both questions were Likert-type scales: 1=very low; 5=very high; 6=don't know. We created a trichotomous variable in which participants whose beliefs and recall were

were coded as accepting the information; participants whose beliefs were

than their recall were coded as underestimating their risk; and those whose beliefs were

than their recall were coded as overestimating their risk. We excluded “

” responses (

=16). Risk recall and risk beliefs were the first and third items in the post-intervention survey. All participants completed these items within two minutes of viewing their personalized diabetes risk information.

Although we provided participants with their risk of several diseases, we can examine risk skepticism only in the context of diabetes. Due to concern about participant burden, we elected in the parent study to include risk recall and belief items only for diabetes.

Information Evaluation Skills

The survey included three variables related to information evaluation skills. We assessed

formal education

with a single item (vocational-technical degree or less; some college or Associate degree; Bachelor's degree; more than Bachelor's degree). We assessed

with a three-item scale (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R39

), adapted to the health context (range 0–3 correct), and

graph literacy

using the four-item Short Graph Literacy Scale (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R40

) (range 0–4 correct). We analyzed each variable separately.

Motivated Reasoning

We assessed

spontaneous self-affirmation

with a single item (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R41

): “When I feel threatened or anxious, I find myself thinking about my values. 1=Do not agree at all; 5=Agree completely.” Spontaneous self-affirmation is a self-report measure of an individual difference stemming from self-affirmation theory, which suggests that people are generally motivated to think of themselves as competent and good (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R42

). Meta-analytic work demonstrates that people who are asked to self-affirm—i.e., to reflect on an important value or strength—report greater acceptance of health messages than those who do not self-affirm (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R43

). More recent research has suggested that individual differences in spontaneous self-affirmation are a psychological resource that helps individuals to cope with threat by restoring a sense of self-integrity (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R44

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R45

We also assessed

information avoidance

with a single item (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R41

): “I avoid stories about diseases from media sources such as TV, the Internet, newspapers, and radio. 1=Do not agree at all; 5=Agree completely.”

Negative affective attitude towards exercise

was assessed with three items (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R46

): “Getting regular exercise is \[enjoyable/unpleasant/fun\]. 1=Do not agree at all; 4=Agree a lot.” The items

were reverse-scored and the items were averaged (α=0.85).

Negative affect about the risk information provided

was assessed with two items: “Think back to when the app showed you your chances of getting the diseases. How \[bad/good\] do you feel about the results? 1=Not \[bad/good\] at all; 5=Extremely \[bad/good\]?” The

item was reverse coded, and the items were averaged;

Bayesian Updating

We assessed

surprise about the risk information provided

with a single item: “How surprised do you feel about the results? 1=Not surprised at all 5=Extremely surprised?”

Personal Relevance Based on Racial and Ethnic Identity

In the risk assessment survey, participants self-reported

(American Indian or Alaska Native; Asian or Pacific Islander; Black or African American; Native Hawaiian; white; two or more races) and

(Hispanic or Latino; not Hispanic or Latino). We dichotomized responses: non-Hispanic white and member of a racial or ethnic group that has been excluded or underrepresented in biomedical research (hereafter

underrepresented

). As mentioned in the introduction, we define personal relevance for this study based on racial and ethnic identity because there may be justifiable concerns about the validity of risk prediction models among people from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups.

Demographic Characteristics

In the risk assessment survey, participants self-reported

(categorized as follows: 30–40; 41–50; and 51–64),

(man; woman), and

comorbidities

: “Have you ever been told you have any of the following \[high blood pressure (hypertension)/high blood cholesterol/heart disease/any type of cancer (other than non-melanoma skin cancer)/stroke/benign breast disease/diabetes or a problem with blood sugar (do not count “prediabetes”)\].” We categorized participants as having 0, 1, or 2 or more comorbidities.

Statistical Analysis

We note deviations from the preregistration. First, we did not test two planned hypotheses that required sub-group analyses that were under-powered. Second, negative affect about the risk information provided was erroneously preregistered as being related to violation of Bayesian reasoning instead of motivated reasoning. Third, we erroneously preregistered surprise as being a moderator of the relationship between diabetes risk information and risk skepticism instead of a potential mediator (see

Supplemental Analyses section

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

We used multinomial logistic regression to analyze the data. In all analyses, the trichotomous risk skepticism variable was the outcome. The predictors were the variables that were intended to capture the explanations under study (e.g., negative affect). We first conducted unadjusted analyses, in which each predictor was examined separately. For hypotheses that included moderation, we added an interaction term for the two variables that were hypothesized to have an interactive relationship with risk skepticism. Next, we tested whether the trichotomous risk skepticism variable was influenced by the three-level risk display variable from the parent intervention. Because risk display was not associated with risk skepticism, we do not discuss it further. We next conducted a single multinomial logistic regression, in which we entered all of the variables that were statistically significant predictors of risk skepticism in the unadjusted analysis (except the diabetes risk information variable). We excluded diabetes risk information from the adjusted analysis because including the information that elicits the cognitive, motivational, and affective responses that result in acceptance or skepticism in the same model as the variables that assess cognitive and affective responses could inadvertently obscure the effects of other explanations for risk skepticism (i.e., there could be an indirect effect of risk information on risk skepticism through the cognitive and affective responses; see

Supplemental Analyses

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

Most participants in this sample were women (85.1%), identified as non-Hispanic white (59.0%), had at least a bachelor's degree (59.3%), had no comorbidities (65.2%), were on average age 46.3 years (SD=9.8, Range=30–64), and were categorized as having low diabetes risk (

=1.2, Median=2.0, Range=1–5). The sample had low-to-moderate numeracy (

=1.0, Median=2.0, Range=0–3) and graph literacy (

=1.1, Median=3.0, Range=0–4). Compared to participants who were included in these analyses, participants who were excluded were more often older, men, members of underrepresented racial or ethnic groups, or they had less formal education, lower numeracy, lower graph literacy, more comorbidities, or higher diabetes risk,

In brief, the trichotomous risk skepticism outcome was statistically significantly associated with numeracy, diabetes risk information, negative affect towards the risk information, feeling surprised about the risk information, being a member of an underrepresented racial or ethnic group, and gender. However, the relationships among those variables were not always in the hypothesized direction. For example, we had hypothesized that higher numeracy would be associated with less overestimation (vs. acceptance). However, we found the opposite relationship (see

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#T2

). In addition, spontaneous self-affirmation and information avoidance were not significant moderators of the association between diabetes risk information and risk skepticism. Education, graph literacy, negative affective attitudes toward exercise, age, and number of comorbidities were not significantly associated with risk skepticism.

Adjusted Analyses

Each predictor that was statistically significantly associated with the trichotomous risk skepticism outcome in the unadjusted analyses remained statistically significant in the adjusted analyses (for full statistical details, see

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#T6

). The directions of the associations between variables in the statistically significant adjusted analyses were similar to those in the unadjusted analysis. Specifically, in contrast to the

information evaluation skills hypothesis

, higher (vs. lower) numeracy remained associated with higher odds of overestimating risk than accepting risk, and there continued to be no association between numeracy and underestimating (

accepting) risk. In partial support of the

motivated reasoning hypothesis

, participants with higher (vs. lower) negative affect towards diabetes risk information had higher odds of underestimating their risk than accepting their risk and underestimating vs. overestimating their risk. In partial support of the

Bayesian reasoning hypothesis

, participants who felt more (vs. less) surprise about the diabetes risk information had higher odds of overestimating than accepting their risk; however, greater surprise was not associated with underestimating (

accepting) risk. The adjusted analyses partially supported the

personal relevance

hypothesis; being a member of an underrepresented racial or ethnic group was associated with higher odds of underestimating risk than accepting risk. However, in contrast to the unadjusted analyses, being a member of an underrepresented racial or ethnic group was not associated with overestimating risk (vs. accepting). Finally, being a woman (vs. man) was associated with higher odds of overestimating risk, but was not associated with underestimating risk. See

Online Supplemental Materials Section C

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

for model fit statistics for all models.

We also conducted a sensitivity analysis to evaluate whether people who recalled their risk correctly (55%,

=197) responded differently than those who recalled their risk incorrectly. The effect of correct recall on the trichotomous risk skepticism outcome was just under the conventional (although arbitrary)

=.05 cutoff, Wald X

=.049. Specifically, compared to participants who incorrectly recalled their risk, those who correctly recalled their risk had lower odds of underestimating than overestimating their risk (OR: 0.44, 95% CI 0.23, 0.85). However, correct vs. incorrect recall was not statistically significantly associated with the underestimated vs. accurate comparison or the overestimated vs. accurate comparison.

Supplemental analyses

Although not described in our preregistration, we explored the possibility of an indirect effect of diabetes risk information on risk skepticism through negative affect and surprise about the risk information provided. We found no statistically significant indirect effects of diabetes risk information on risk underestimation vs. acceptance, on risk overestimation vs. acceptance, or on risk underestimation vs. overestimation through either negative affect or surprise about the risk information provided (see

Online Supplementary Materials Section C

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

for detailed statistical information). We also found no evidence that negative affect and surprise acted as parallel indirect effects.

We report three key findings from our exploration of possible explanations for skepticism of personalized diabetes risk information. First, consistent with other research related to communicating personalized health risk information (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R4

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R14

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R47

), risk skepticism was common; approximately 58% of participants expressed skepticism of the personalized diabetes risk information they were provided. Second, risk skepticism could happen in both “directions.” Few studies have separated people who are skeptical of personalized risk information because they believe it is too high

too low (but see (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R13

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R48

) ); instead they combine both groups of people into a single “risk skepticism” category. This could be problematic if, as we show in our research, a given explanation might apply differentially to risk overestimators and underestimators. Our third key message is that the cognitive, motivational, and affective factors driving risk skepticism are complex and nuanced, which may be critical for designing better risk communication messages and for identifying opportunities for improving precision medicine (e.g., increase the racial and ethnic diversity of the cohorts used to create the risk prediction models to increase perceived personal relevance and acceptance among socio-demographic groups that have been marginalized).

The unadjusted, adjusted, and indirect effects analyses lead us to conclude that risk skepticism is more likely to be grounded in affective, motivational, or experiential phenomena than on knowledge alone (see also (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R49

)). Only one of six analyses supported information evaluation skills as a possible explanation for risk skepticism. In contrast, to the extent that participants were told they were at higher risk of diabetes, they also expressed more negative affect about the information they were given (

< .001). In addition, as predicted, negative affect about the results was associated with greater underestimation of risk than either acceptance of or overestimation of risk (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#T2

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#T3

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#T5

). These findings are consistent with the pattern of results that would be expected from a motivated reasoning explanation (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R17

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R18

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R50

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R51

), whereby threatening personally-relevant health risk information prompts people to attempt to alleviate negative affect by asserting that their actual risk is lower than the information provided to them. Negative affect in response to risk information may prompt counterargumentation defenses (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

However, there was also evidence suggesting constraints on motivated reasoning as an explanation. Whereas prior research suggests that risk skepticism may be more common if accepting the information would require engaging in an undesired behavior (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R20

), negative affective attitudes toward exercise were not associated with risk skepticism. Also contrary to hypotheses, the effect of personalized risk information on risk skepticism was not moderated by spontaneous self-affirmation or information avoidance tendencies (although it is possible that individuals high in tendency to avoid health information may have self-selected out of participating in the study, in an attempt to avoid learning about health information entirely; such a selection bias could have obscured any effect of information avoidance on risk skepticism). We also did not find an indirect effect of diabetes risk information on risk skepticism through negative affect about the risk information provided. However, we have concerns about statistical power for the tests of mediation (in which

=214 for the underestimation vs. acceptance analysis, and

=205 for the underestimation vs. overestimation analysis) and moderation (in which only

=63 participants underestimated their risk). Therefore, we are hesitant to rule out motivated reasoning as a possible explanation without additional data from studies that have larger sample sizes and use experimental designs.

The findings related to surprise suggest that risk skepticism may be associated with Bayesian updating only for risk overestimation, not underestimation. Other research also reports surprise and skepticism among people who are told they are at low risk of a negative health outcome when they were expecting to be told they were high risk (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R7

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R9

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R13

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R52

). However, we did not ask participants directly whether they were surprised because the risk information was higher or lower than they expected. This more detailed information about

participants were surprised would have been helpful for interpreting the findings. For example, it is possible for two people to indicate feeling surprised but for different reasons (e.g., one person told they were at low risk when they were expecting to learn they were at high risk, and the other told they were at high risk when they were expecting to see low risk). Therefore, we view these findings as preliminary support for the Bayesian updating perspective. Additional research that examines expectations, rather than surprise, is needed to draw a more definitive conclusion.

Unfortunately, we did not include a direct measure of personal relevance, and this makes it difficult to interpret the findings about personal relevance as a possible explanation for risk skepticism. Nevertheless, it is not unreasonable to expect that members of racial and ethnic groups that are underrepresented in research are aware of such underrepresentation (despite comprising 13% of the U.S. population, only 4.5% of clinical trial participants from 2008–2018 were Black) (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R53

). This could produce skepticism about the relevance of biomedical research findings. For example, when asked to evaluate a news article reporting the discovery of a gene associated with increased risk of nicotine addiction, several Black participants asked whether Black people were included in the research and indicated skepticism about whether a study comprised mostly of white people would apply to Black people (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R26

). However, this does not explain why being a member of an underrepresented group was associated with only risk underestimation and not overestimation. One possible alternative explanation to personal relevance is related to trust; other researchers have reported that, compared to patients who have low trust in their physicians, patients who have high trust may be more likely to accept “bad news,” such as being informed that they are at high risk of developing a disease (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R54

). African Americans, who comprise the largest proportion of people from underrepresented groups in this study, have many reasons to mistrust the U.S. biomedical research establishment (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R55

); this mistrust may have been expressed as skepticism of high-risk information, resulting in underestimation of risk.

An unexpected finding was that women were more likely than men to overestimate (vs. accept) their personalized risk information. This is consistent with reports from other studies, which reported that women tend to have higher risk perceptions than men (or, conversely, that men have lower risk perceptions than women) (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R56

). This difference, often referred to as the “white male” effect (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R57

), is thought to protect white men's identities as people who are individualists and who have high social status. For more information about the role of individualism, hierarchical beliefs, and risk perceptions, see (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R58

). Research that seeks greater understanding of how gender influences risk skepticism or acceptance could contribute to identifying, understanding, and reducing gender-based health disparities.

Limitations and Future Directions

These results should be considered in light of the following limitations. First, we used single-item measures, and we were not able to include all the measures needed to draw firm conclusions about which explanation or explanations produced risk skepticism (e.g., personal relevance and trust in the medical system). In addition, because we calculated sample size based on the needs of the RCT and not this particular set of analyses, the tests of mediation and moderation may be underpowered and should be replicated in future research. Second, although we had a large proportion of the sample identify as Black or African American, representation from people from other underrepresented racial or ethnic groups, and from people with limited formal schooling, was limited. In addition, the individuals excluded from the analyses due to missing data were disproportionately members of groups that experience health disparities. Thus, the generalizability of these findings to a wide variety of socio-demographic groups is limited. Third, although we measured health literacy, we did so using the Single Item Health Screener (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R59

), which is better attuned to identifying people with very limited health literacy, rather than a range of literacy levels. As a result, the sample's health literacy was so high (i.e., 96% reported never or rarely needing help understanding written health materials) that we were concerned about ceiling effects obscuring our findings. Fourth, the analyses were cross-sectional, limiting our ability to infer directionality and causality, and preventing us from determining whether and how risk skepticism changes over time. Fifth, although we included attention check items to ensure high data quality (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R60

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R61

), doing so may have inadvertently influenced responses in unknown ways (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R62

Online Supplemental Materials, Section A

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#SD1

for details about these items. Sixth, it should be noted that the disproportionate percentage of people who overestimated

underestimated their risk in the overall sample could have occurred, in part, because the diabetes risk estimates provided to participants were generally low, so there was less room available in the scale for them to underestimate. Future research should explore whether disproportionate rates are due to this possible methodological artifact or some other reason (e.g., bracing for bad news; avoiding “tempting fate”). Finally, because the purpose of the parent study was to increase understanding of the importance of physical activity for a variety of health outcomes, we did not instruct participants to focus specifically on the diabetes risk information. Thus, they could have been thinking of other health conditions while answering the survey items.

One key implication of these findings for risk communication is that, although it is generally important to present risk information in ways that are accessible and understandable to people with limited formal education, numeracy, and health literacy, such efforts are unlikely to reduce risk skepticism. Rather, to obtain insights into the specific risk communication formats and strategies that might reduce risk skepticism (e.g., numbers vs. words, percent vs. frequency, narrative vs. didactic), it will be necessary to gain additional understanding of the risk skepticism phenomenon itself. Thus, studies are needed whose primary purpose is to identify the mechanisms driving risk skepticism under varying conditions. This includes research that involves a longitudinal assessment of any change in skepticism, is adequately powered for complex statistical analyses, and includes broader socio-demographic representation, a more sensitive measure of health literacy, and validated, multi-item measures, including measures of perceived personal relevance and trust in biomedical research. It might also be worth adding questions to assess whether knowledge of disease risk factors contributes to risk skepticism. Such research should also acknowledge – and ideally be designed to detect – the possibility that risk skepticism is driven by either multiple mechanisms simultaneously, or by different mechanisms under different conditions. For example, Bayesian updating might be a strong influence on risk skepticism when a person receives a lower personalized risk estimate than expected, but motivated reasoning might be more influential if the estimate is very high. That said, it is also possible that laypeople do not need fine-grained distinctions in risk to make health decisions; perhaps they simply need to feel at risk for a negative health outcome (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R63

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R64

). Future work could explore this issue by varying the specificity of risk information and evaluating behavioral outcomes. Future work could also examine how variability in interpretation of verbal risk labels affects expression of risk skepticism and possible explanations of skepticism. It is also worth asking whether mechanisms of risk skepticism are similar or different for different health conditions. For instance, is motivated reasoning a more powerful explanation for conditions that are highly feared, like cancer, compared to less severe conditions like osteoporosis? It may also be worth exploring whether the explanations presented in this study influence risk recall itself, particularly as time passes between when the risk information is provided and when risk recall and belief are assessed. Altogether, such a body of research (together with existing theorizing (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R22

) and thinking (

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164692/#R15

) on this issue) could contribute to the development of a formal theoretical framework of risk skepticism and eventually shape clinical and public health practice.

Conclusions

We compared four possible explanations for skepticism of personalized diabetes risk information. Our findings suggest that information evaluation skills are unlikely to be a main driver of risk skepticism. We also found preliminary evidence supporting motivated reasoning and Bayesian updating as possible explanations. Finally, we determined that racial and ethnic identity are likely important for risk skepticism. These results have important implications for health communication. Simply providing people with personalized diabetes risk information is unlikely to result in immediate acceptance of the information. Rather, it is more likely that people will be skeptical of than accept their risk. To develop more effective interventions and risk messages, it is important to understand

people accept or are skeptical of their risk.

Social Media Content.

Most people who received personalized diabetes risk information did not believe it was accurate for themselves.

Skepticism of personalized risk information does not appear to be due to people's inability to understand the information provided.

Simply providing people with personalized diabetes risk information is unlikely to result in immediate acceptance of the information

). We chose the term

because it best reflects the possibility that people could come to accept the information in the future upon more reflection or the receipt of new information (although this study was not designed to test temporal changes or trends in skepticism).
