RESPONSE TO REVIEWER 2

Dear Reviewer #2,

Thank you for your mindful reading of the manuscript and for your suggestions. We have implemented all of the recommendations you made except for # 2 and #5. Point # 2 was about using the weighted mean and not the arithmetic mean for the dependent variable perception of immigration. This suggestion, which is normally valid, turned out to be unnecessary in this particular case. We have justified our choice in detail and stand ready to modify the analyses if you deem it necessary. As for point #5 we also explained our reasons below, but we are open in case you prefer to include the results in the manuscript or in the Supporting information. All other suggestions have been implemented, and because of this, we think the manuscript is much improved. Thanks.

The study investigated whether individuals' numerical ability, scientific and economic literacy impact their perception of immigration, taking into account their cultural worldview. The PRI survey used a questionnaire with standardized and ad hoc questions. A representative sample of 551 citizens of a town in the northeast of Italy, thus not a national sample. I found the paper interesting and I think the practical implications that can be derived are very important. Although it was a fairly smooth read, I think there are aspects to consider to improve its quality.

ANSWER: We're glad you found the work interesting.

I think that the variable Perception of Immigration could have been computed more accurately, considering the weight of every single item. It would be advisable to report Cronbach's alpha index in addition to proceeding with factor analysis.

ANSWER: Sorry for not being able to communicate these things clearly enough in the manuscript. Actually, Cronbach's alpha was calculated (� = .94), but it is now reported in the paper more clearly. Also, the way the dependent variable 'perception of immigration' was constructed has been made clearer. We explained that the immigration perception variable is the simple arithmetic mean (individual by individual) of the scores given by each respondent to 13 opinion questions about immigrants. We clarified that, before performing the calculation of the averages, the scales of some variables were reversed so that higher scores correspond to a more "favorable" position on immigration. More importantly, a PCA was performed as you suggested but we feel it is not necessary to report this analysis in the main manuscript (although we make it available in the SI) and would prefer to use the mean and not the weighted mean, for three reasons:

(1) the arithmetic mean results in less loss of information and, therefore, greater "recovery" of data; in fact, PCA uses complete data and any partial non-response imposes exclusion from the calculation of the record for the individual who did not answer one or more questions. Below are the results of PCA, which we would prefer not to report in the manuscript, not without first showing the correlation matrices constructed by calculating Sperman's � (if we are to consider the nature of the data, which are to all ranks) and Pearson's linear correlation coefficients r.

(3) The average of the 13 variables we have calculated shows a very high correlation with the score given by the first main component (the so-called scores, i.e. the values of the new variable defined, precisely, by the first main component). This correlation, measured with Pearson's linear correlation coefficient r, is equal to 0.98 approximately. Below we also report the scatter of our dependent variable Y against the scores attributed by the first principal component:

In conclusion, we feel that this evidence supports the choice of using the arithmetic mean of the 13 questions to construct the dependent variable perception of immigration, which is more intuitive and more "informative" than the first main component. Summing, and then averaging, the answers given by the respondents to the 13 questions that contribute to the construction of the variable Y is a good strategy, also because of the "I do not know/do not answer". In the manuscript we have added, in this regard, a clarification in the method section and made the statistics available in the supplementary materials (Tables S6 and S7):

" To be conservative, the 13 items were subjected to a principal component analysis which showed that the principal component explains about 60% of the total variability and that the weights of the items (the factor loadings of the PCA) are substantially equal to each other. In addition, the arithmetic mean of the 13 items has a very high correlation index (r = .98) with the score given by the first principal component (the scores, i.e., the values of the new variable defined, precisely, by the first principal component). We, therefore, considered it more informative to use the simple arithmetic mean as the dependent variable and not a more complex statistic, such as the mean of the items each weighted by the principal component, also because the arithmetic mean entails a lesser loss of information due to missing cases."

If I understand Table 1 correctly, the models are represented by a column. However, I found Table 1 to be unintuitive and hard to read. I suggest replacing the indices b0, b1, etc with the predictors considered in the 4 models.

ANSWER: We did it. The same concern was raised by another reviewer. As suggested, we made explicit the variable to which lines b0, b1, b2, and b3 in Table 1 refer: the intercept, the literacy variable, the worldviews, and the interaction, respectively.

In addition, I think it would be useful to do an analysis to indicate which of the 4 tested models is the best (e.g., ANOVA or AIC).

ANSWER: We included AIC values in the last row of Table 1 and commented on them in the text as follows:

" The last row of Table 1 shows the AIC (Akaike information criterion) values for the four fitted models. The model with the lowest AIC included total literacy as the explanatory variable, while the model with the highest AIC included numeracy as the explanatory variable. The difference between these two AICs was 7.651, indicating, according to Burnham and Anderson (2004), good support for considering the model that included total literacy as an explanatory variable as a better model. A similar result, even if with weaker evidence, was found when considering the AIC difference between this model and those which included economic literacy (3.137) or science literacy (5.658) as the explanatory variable"

Further, I think it would be interesting, also for the practical implications of the study, to have a model that simultaneously estimates the effect of numeracy, economic, and science literacy, unless they have a strong correlation with each other (in which case it should be specified).

ANSWER: Yes, the request makes sense. On the one hand, the three variables are quite related:

#### Results show that:

When z = 0 we have that the expected values are given by 2.95 + 0.031xeconomic + 0.097xnumeracy

When z = 1 we have that the expected values are given by (2.95-0.16) + 0.031xeconomic + (0.097-0.15)x numeracy. Thus, with economic being equal, as numeracy increases, the predicted values in the group with z=0 grow, while in the group with z=1, again with economic being equal, as numeracy increases, the predicted values decrease (or rather, remain essentially constant).

In both groups (z=0 and z=1), with equal numeracy, as economic increases, the expected values increase (in the same way in both groups). In both groups (z=0 and z=1), at equal numeracy and economic, the predicted values do not depend on science.

Given these results, we believe it is more elegant to show a separate model for each predictor. Indeed, the purpose of our work was not to have a competition among predictors to see which among the three predictors was more powerful in determining the effect but rather to observe how each determined the effect. The three predictors, in our view, measure related but also very different, constructs, otherwise, we would not have studied all three of them. In the introductory part of the paper we expand on each of them by noting how each has its own distinctive features in relation to the immigration issue. In conclusion, we believe the proposed solution with the three predictors examined in three separate models is better. However, if the editor prefers, we can easily edit or include also this analysis in the manuscript.

Since you decide to investigate cultural worldview instead of using political orientation, I would suggest discussing it more in deep. For example, are there any studies investigating the correlation between the two measures? This could help support your choice of not considering the political orientation and polarization, even if the Italian political situation is very "confused". I suggest that the link between polarization and cultural worldview is discussed more fully already in the introduction.

ANSWER: Sorry for the confusion. We did write that we decided to investigate cultural worldview instead of using political orientation but we did not mean it, literally. To be more clear, we choose to measure worldviews not as a "substitute" or "proxy" of political worldviews but because we believed that they were better suited to measure knowledge-related polarization, than political orientation, when dealing with attitudes and behaviors in front of threats (such as immigration). As you suggested we now have detailed our arguments in the paper, both in the introduction and in the conclusion sections.

#### In the introduction:

Most studies on the polarization of beliefs used political orientation as the polarizing variable. Instead, following Kahan et al. (2012), we used a more nuanced underlying ideological measure, i.e., worldviews, to capture where the individual lies on the ideological spectrum represented by hierarchical-individualistic views on one side and egalitarian-communitarian views on the other. Individual preferences on social problems such as gun control, nuclear waste disposals, COVID-19, and climate change are strongly influenced by cultural worldviews (Cherry et al., 2017; Dryhurst et al., 2020; Kahan et al., 2011; Siegrist & Bearth, 2021). Indeed, in a study of 6,991 individuals across the world, an individualistic worldview predicted COVID-19-related attitudes and behaviors more than all other variables (including political orientation) in five out of the ten countries surveyed (UK, Germany, Sweden, Spain, and Japan) (Dryhurst et al., 2020). Moreover, worldviews have been successfully used in a prior study on risk perception and the polarizing impact of knowledge (Kahan, 2012). We, therefore, measured individual worldviews to categorize individuals into hierarchical-individualistic vs. egalitarian-communitarian and measure the polarizing impact that this underlying ideology induces when put in interaction with personal knowledge..

#### In the conclusions:

" Many studies have used a measure of political orientation to elicit the knowledge-related polarization effect (Drummond & Fischhoff, 2017; Hamilton et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2017). While in some cases this has been a pre-designed choice (e.g., Shoots-Reinhard et al., 2021), in other cases such as large-scale representative surveys, it has been an ex-post forced choice due to its availability (e.g., Drummond & Fischhoff, 2017). In deciding the ideological measure to use in our study we decided to avoid using political orientation. Political orientation is typically elicited by asking respondents to classify themselves on some bipolar dimension, such as, republican vs. democrat or liberal vs. conservative. Instead, we preferred to use a measure of cultural worldviews (Kahan et al., 2011). The reason for this choice was twofold. On the one hand, a standard question about political orientation (right-wing or left-wing) would not adapt well to our context. Indeed, the Italian political landscape is characterized by small and fragmented parties with transversal positions with respect to the standard right-wing or left-wing dichotomy. For example, the 5 Star Movement is a populist party difficult to classify as right or left (Roccato et al., 2020; Verbeek & Zaslove, 2016). It has both right-wing (e.g., anti-immigrant) and left-wing (e.g., guaranteed minimum income) ideologies, as well as both conservative (e.g., NO TAV movement) and liberal (e.g., drug liberalization) ideologies (Roccato et al., 2020). A second and more important reason is that we believe worldviews are a more detailed and nuanced measure of the underlying ideology of individual beliefs and behaviors than political orientation, with whom they do not fully overlap. Worldviews capture where an individual stands on the spectrum anchored by hierarchical-individualistic beliefs at one pole and egalitarian-communitarian beliefs at the other. They have proved to be successful in identifying a knowledge-related polarizing effect in the case of previous risk perception studies (Kahan 2912). Moreover, worldview orientations have been shown to be significant predictors of an individual's attitudes and behaviors in the face of threats (Chen et al., 2020; Siegrist & Bearth, 2021; Xue et al., 2014), sometimes even more than political orientations (Dryhurst et al., 2020). Our study confirms that cultural worldviews may be a valid construct for measuring knowledge-related polarization effects of risk perceptions of social problems

In the state of the art, I would anticipate (briefly) why the numeracy, economic, and science literacy scales were chosen as variables. I believe that this clarification can be helpful in the reading.

ANSWER: This was an excellent advise, thank you. In the State of the Art we have now included a paragraph which anticipates the decision to measure the three predictors (science, economic and number literacy). The paragraph is the following:

" Of central importance to the knowledge-related polarization effect is the type of knowledge/education/ability considered in the interaction (Shoots-Reinhard et al., 2021). Across studies on polarization, researchers have mostly used education as the knowledge variable to test for the interaction between partnership and opinions, with few exceptions that used science knowledge and others that used cognitive abilities (i.e., numeracy and verbal abilities). The type of knowledge variable chosen has been shown to determine the chance of detecting the interaction with ideology (Shoots-Reinhard et al., 2021). When verbal ability measures were not controlled for, numeracy and ideology did interact to predict outcomes, but they failed to interact when the verbal ability measure was included in the model (Shoots-Reinhard et al., 2021). Thus in the present study, we chose to examine the hypothesized interaction effect (knowledge x ideology), exploring multiple knowledge variables. We used two knowledge predictors (science and economic literacy) and one cognitive ability predictor (numeracy) to broaden the set of knowledge variables that elicit the knowledge-related polarization effect.

About science literacy (paragraph 2.4), I would add some references (also from newspapers) to justify the passage on the intertwining between migrants and the increase of viral infections.

ANSWER: You're right, we make a lot of statements but don't support them with adequate references. We have now added references. We believe the paragraph is much improved now:

" Science literacy is the knowledge of basic scientific facts (National Science Board & National Science Foundation, 2020). While scientific knowledge is usually not a significant predictor of risk perception per se (Ho et al., 2019; Kahan et al., 2012), it is a significant factor in polarizing public opinions about climate change (Drummond & Fischhoff, 2017; Kahan et al., 2012). Individuals with higher science literacy showed the greatest cultural-worldviews polarization for climate change risks (Kahan et al., 2012). Seemingly, individuals with greater science knowledge showed more political polarization on issues such as stem cell research, the big bang, human evolution, and climate change (Drummond & Fischhoff, 2017). On a similar line, greater attention to scientific news increased support for policies aimed at reducing climate change for strong liberals but reduced support for strong conservatives (Hart et al., 2015). Science knowledge and fear of immigration share a common ground when it comes to viruses and diseases. Indeed, people might fear immigrants thinking that they can be vehicles for viruses and diseases. Concerns about immigrants and disease have been constantly registered throughout history. For example, Merkel and Stern (2002) explored why in three periods, from 1880 to the present, immigrants have been stigmatized as the etiology of a variety of diseases, despite the data do not support such a narrative. Human mobility, indeed, was historically associated with the spread of infectious diseases (Castelli & Sulis, 2017), however this relationship no longer existing in the contemporary age. Despite this, fear is still supported by the media who portray immigrants as disease spreaders (Esses et al., 2013). For example, during the of COVID-19 outbreak in Italy, the question of whether more immigrants should be brought into the country from the sea borders was also deeply intertwined with the threat they posed as positive drivers of viral infection (Rowe et al., 2021). However, this might be especially true for individuals opposing immigration who historically hold a more ideological attitude of right-wing authoritarianism. We, therefore, predicted that greater science knowledge would interact with cultural worldview orientations in explaining public opinion on immigration. Thus, we anticipated those people with greater science knowledge, and egalitarian-communitarian orientation might show more extreme positive opinions on immigration, while those people with greater science knowledge and hierarchical-individualistic orientation might show more strong negative opinions on immigration. “

Thanks for the suggestions and thanks for your careful reading.

Reviewer #1: I found this manuscript to be much improved. I especially appreciated the thoughtful and convincing response to the dichotomization issue--the extra explanation and analyses were extremely helpful. It seems possible that Kahan's cultural worldview measure might be more predictive cross-culturally than liberal/conservative scales that are so prevalent in the U.S. and could be another factor in predicting when and for whom people higher in intelligence/knowledge/literacy are more polarized. Predicting that polarization is predicated on being able to measure the variable motivating the polarization in the first place. I think that if you wanted to, you could study this in future research. It may be another factor explaining why some researchers have not found polarization--perhaps they are measuring the wrong worldview (i.e., liberal/conservative vs. egalitarian/hierarchical).

Why Facts Lose to Emotions

Maksym Skubenko

https://voxukraine.org/en/authors/maksym-skubenko

https://voxukraine.org/en/category/society-en

Photo: unsplash.com / Ryoji Iwata

February 26, 2026

https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fvoxukraine.org%2Fen%2Fwhy-facts-lose-to-emotions

https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fvoxukraine.org%2Fen%2Fwhy-facts-lose-to-emotions&text=Why%20Facts%20Lose%20to%20Emotions

https://t.me/share/url?url=https%3A%2F%2Fvoxukraine.org%2Fen%2Fwhy-facts-lose-to-emotions&text=Why%20Facts%20Lose%20to%20Emotions

The science of disinformation: what works, what does not, and why this matters right now. A review of current research on countering disinformation.

In 2018, a group of researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

https://ide.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/2017-IDE-Research-Brief-False-News.pdf

126,000 news cascades on Twitter (now X), shared by around three million users. The result was striking: false news spread faster, deeper, and more widely than true news. Moreover, the most dramatic gap was not in medicine or finance, but in politics.

Most notably, bots accelerated the spread of both true and false news at

roughly the same rate

. Falsehood prevailed not because of technology, but because of people. False news triggered surprise, fear, and disgust, whereas the truth elicited sadness, predictability, and trust. In other words, false stories spread more successfully because they are more emotionally compelling than the truth.

https://politics.media.mit.edu/papers/Vosoughi\_Science.pdf

by Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy, and Sinan Aral, published in

, became one of the most cited scientific papers of 2018. More importantly, over the following six years, its findings were confirmed, extended, and refined by dozens of subsequent studies. It is these studies that are now reshaping our understanding of how to counter disinformation.

Why smart people believe nonsense

The intuitive explanation is straightforward: people believe fake stories because they lack knowledge or education. The “science literacy model,” which dominated efforts to counter disinformation for decades, holds that the solution is to educate people, present evidence, and correct errors. However, more recent research shows that this model is incorrect — or, at the very least, seriously incomplete.

In 2017, Dan Kahan of Yale University

https://rcgd.isr.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/motivated\_numeracy\_and\_enlightened\_selfgovernment.pdf

what is known as

identity-protective cognition

and identified a paradox: intelligent, well-educated individuals do not become more objective on contentious political issues. On the contrary, they defend their group's position even more firmly. They deploy their cognitive abilities not to seek the truth, but to justify what they already believe.

Participants were given a task involving interpreting numerical data from a table: they had to determine which conclusion actually followed from the evidence. In different versions of the experiment, the same mathematical structure was linked to a politically sensitive topic — one with which participants associated themselves with a particular camp (for example, left or right, conservative or liberal, and so on).

When the correct answer aligned with the position typical of the participant's own political camp, individuals with stronger mathematical or analytical skills were more likely to answer correctly. However, when the correct conclusion conflicted with a position central to their group identity, those same individuals were more likely to reach an incorrect conclusion or interpret the data selectively.

Gordon Pennycook and David G. Rand (2019,

) reached a somewhat different conclusion: susceptibility to fake news is better explained not by motivated reasoning, but by insufficient cognitive effort. In other words, people believe fake news not because they interpret it through the lens of their prior beliefs (identity-protective cognition), but because they fail to evaluate it critically. Across two

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S001002771830163X?via%3Dihub

(total sample N = 3,446), the authors found that analytic thinking helps individuals distinguish fake news from accurate information, regardless of political orientation. The problem, therefore, is not bias, but insufficient cognitive engagement — what the authors term “lazy thinking.”

These two conclusions do not contradict each other. Rather, they describe different conditions. When a belief has not yet become part of one's identity, it may be sufficient to pause and reflect. However, once it has, even an intelligent person may deploy their full cognitive capacity to defend a false belief.

It is also important to consider the physiological dimension. For example, in 2016, neuroscientists at the University of Southern California — Jonas T. Kaplan, Sarah I. Gimbel, and Sam Harris —

https://www.nature.com/articles/srep39589

that when individuals encounter arguments that challenge their political beliefs, the amygdala and the insular cortex become more active — brain regions associated with threat perception and anxiety. In effect, the brain perceives the refutation of an identity-relevant belief as an attack.

The backfire effect: a fear that proved exaggerated

For many years, communicators and journalists feared the “backfire effect” — the idea that corrections might reinforce false beliefs. This concern discouraged many from engaging in assertive fact-checking.

Contemporary research, however, calls this fear into question. A large

meta-analysis

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-023-01623-8

by Man-Pui Sally Chan and Dolores Albarracín (2023, Nature Human Behaviour), synthesizing 245 estimates from 75 studies (total N = 53,320), found that, on average, the effects of corrections were minimal and statistically insignificant. However, they varied substantially across topics and contexts. The backfire effect appears to be rare and not a systematic consequence of fact-checking. However, there are still relatively few experimental studies assessing the impact of repeated exposure to misinformation or to corrections, and this question therefore requires further investigation.

Briony Swire-Thompson et al. (2022, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General)

https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2Fxge0001131

this line of research. Across two experiments (N = 388 and 532), not a single false claim produced a backfire effect compared with the control group. Moreover, the authors suggested that one reason earlier studies reported backfire effects may have been the unreliability of the measurement instruments.

Brendan Nyhan (2021,

https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117

this most directly: the reason corrections do not always work lies not in backfire effects, but in other factors. These include the rapid decay of correction effects over time, limitations in the targeting of fact-checks, the constant stream of messages from political elites and media promoting more appealing but false claims, and insufficient cognitive effort in information processing. In other words, corrections are both possible and necessary. However, it is unrealistic to expect that a single correction will permanently change a belief.

Ten seconds that change decisions

The Behavioural Insights Team (BIT) conducted a

https://www.bi.team/blogs/what-works-in-disinformation-wars/

in Ukraine in 2019 and found that a simple ten-second pause before assessing the accuracy of a headline significantly reduced the likelihood of believing fake news. The effect was consistent among both Ukrainian- and Russian-speaking participants.

This finding aligns with the conclusions of Pennycook and Rand: part of the problem lies not in ideological bias, but in insufficient cognitive effort. People spend approximately two seconds on social media content before sharing it. An additional eight seconds may be sufficient to activate analytic thinking. On this basis, Pennycook and Rand (2022,

The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science

) developed the concept of “accuracy nudges” — subtle prompts that encourage users to evaluate the accuracy of information before sharing it. Major social media platforms are already testing this approach.

Why Ukraine proved more resilient than expected

Ukraine's resilience to Russian disinformation was examined by Todd Helmus and Khrystyna Holynska (2024, RAND Corporation) in a major

https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research\_reports/RRA2700/RRA2771-1/RAND\_RRA2771-1.pdf

published in 2024. As part of this work, the researchers consulted, among others, representatives of VoxUkraine. One of the central conclusions was that Ukraine's success is linked to the fact that civil society organizations and fact-checking institutions had been established before the full-scale invasion. Trust in these institutions, together with their expertise and coordination, created an infrastructure that cannot be built in the midst of a crisis.

The authors recommend investing in civil society institutions in advance to ensure they possess the trust and resources necessary to counter foreign disinformation. In times of crisis, coordination among the state, the media, and civil society is critically important.

Inoculation theory is not a panacea

Inoculation theory, proposed by William McGuire in the 1960s as a “vaccine against brainwashing,” appeared to offer an ideal solution for the social media era. The logic is simple and elegant: just as a medical vaccine prepares the immune system to encounter a virus, psychological inoculation is intended to prepare the mind to encounter disinformation.

Sander van der Linden and Jon Roozenbeek of the University of Cambridge implemented this idea in the

online game

https://www.getbadnews.com/books/ukrainian/

. Rather than simply teaching facts, they proposed an innovative approach: allowing individuals to create and spread disinformation themselves. In the game, participants learn six classic manipulation techniques (DEPICT): discrediting opponents, using emotional language, polarization, creating fake accounts, promoting conspiracy theories, and trolling.

Explanation: the DEPICT mnemonic

The DEPICT mnemonic (six common manipulative techniques)

In research on the game Bad News, these techniques are commonly referred to by the acronym DEPICT. It serves as a concise reference tool for recognizing manipulation in news and social media:

D—Discredit: attacking an opponent's reputation instead of responding to their argument (an ad hominem attack—shifting the focus to the person). Example: “That's what a sellout would say.”

E—Emotion: using language designed to trigger fear, anger, or disgust, thereby reducing critical scrutiny. Example: “SHOCK! BETRAYAL! Share immediately!”

P—Polarization: framing the world in binary terms—“us” versus “them,” “patriots” versus “traitors”—leaving no room for nuance. Example: “If you're not with us, you're against us.”

I—Impersonation: mimicking or fabricating “official sources,” “experts,” or supposed insider information. Example: fake “orders,” “screenshots,” or “letters” attributed to institutions.

C—Conspiracy: explaining events through a “secret plan” without verifiable evidence. Example: “It was all decided long ago behind closed doors.”

T—Trolling: deliberately provoking emotional reactions and conflict in order to maximize attention and disruption. Example: provocative “hooks” designed to pit groups against one another.

DEPICT describes techniques rather than topics. As a result, the approach functions effectively as a preventive tool: it helps people recognize manipulation even when the specific fake story is new.

The initial results appeared impressive. The early studies involved more than 15,000

participants

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-019-0279-9

, the game was deployed at scale in many countries, and it was translated into more than 20 languages. Participants who played the game subsequently performed better at identifying unreliable tweets and headlines. More than one million people completed the game, and it was featured in leading scientific journals and praised in outlets such as the

https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-43154667

The Telegraph

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2018/02/20/honestly-fake-news-now-online-game-will-help-fight-against/

The Guardian

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2018/feb/20/bad-news-the-game-researchers-hope-will-vaccinate-public-against-fake-news

became a flagship example of evidence-based efforts to counter disinformation.

When the lens changed

However, in 2023, researchers at the University of Southampton — Ariana Modirrousta-Galian and Philip Higham —

https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2023-58664-001

a systematic replication of earlier studies with methodological improvements. This type of research involves repeating an original experiment using a more rigorous methodology. They did not simply replicate the experiments; they applied a more precise analytical approach.

The analysis covered nine studies with different samples, ranging from 110 to 14,000 participants, conducted across multiple countries and using different research designs. Some included a control group, while others did not; some used the same headlines in both the pre-test and post-test, while others used different ones. This variation is important because it allows researchers to assess whether the observed pattern holds regardless of methodological differences.

problem with earlier studies

was that they measured participants'

average ratings

of news reliability before and after playing the game. Indeed, on average, participants rated fake news as less reliable after

. This suggested that the approach was effective.

However, average ratings are like measuring the temperature of a hospital: it may appear normal overall, even if half the patients are freezing and the other half are burning with fever. Instead, the team applied receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis

—a method derived from signal detection theory—allows researchers to distinguish between two components:

Discrimination

— whether a person can DISTINGUISH between fake news and true news.

Response bias

— whether a person tends to rate news as MORE or LESS reliable overall, regardless of its actual accuracy.

When this analysis was applied to all available data from

(including the original studies by Sander van der Linden and Jon Roozenbeek), the picture changed fundamentally.

The table presents two types of indicators. The

-value indicates the probability that the result occurred by chance: the smaller the p-value, the lower the likelihood that the finding is due to random variation, and the more reliable the effect. A value of p < .001 corresponds to less than a 0.1% probability that the result occurred by chance. Cohen's

indicates the effect

https://statisticsbyjim.com/basics/cohens-d/

— that is, the magnitude of the change. As a general guide, d ≤ 0.2 is considered a small effect, 0.2 < d < 0.8 a medium effect, and d ≥ 0.8 a large effect.

Improved discrimination?

Shift toward skepticism?

Roozenbeek and van der Linden (2019)

(p<.001, d=0.47)

Basol et al. (2020)

(p<.001, d=1.40)

Martens et al. (2021)

(p<.001, d=0.87)

Roozenbeek et al. (2022)

(p<.001, d=0.37)

Graham et al. (2023)

(p<.001), effect size was not assessed

In the discrimination column—that is, the ability to distinguish true from fake news—p-values are large throughout. None of the studies demonstrated a statistically reliable improvement in discrimination. By contrast, in the response bias column—that is, shifts in the overall trust threshold—p < .001 appears in most cases, and effect sizes are sometimes very large, reaching d = 1.40 in Martens et al. (2021). In Graham et al. (2023), the effect size for response bias could not be calculated due to incomplete underlying data; however, the statistical significance of the shift (p < .001) was confirmed.

did not, in fact, improve participants' ability to distinguish between fake news and true news. Instead, the game primarily increased general

skepticism toward all news

, both false and true. Chan Lu and colleagues

https://www.jmir.org/2025/1/e80134

a similar conclusion, finding that

reduced trust in accurate news.

Why this is critically important

#### Consider two individuals after the COVID-19 infodemic:

#### Person A (better at distinguishing fake news—higher discrimination):

Sees: “5G towers cause COVID-19” → “This is a fake story” ✓

Sees: “Vaccination protects against severe COVID-19” → “This is true” ✓

#### Person B (generally skeptical toward news—conservative response bias):

Sees: “5G towers cause COVID-19” → “I don't believe it” ✓

Sees: “Vaccination protects against severe COVID-19” → “I don't believe it” ✗

produces Person B, not Person A.

#### This is problematic for three reasons:

Most of the news people encounter is accurate.

For example, a

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-020-0833-x

of online news consumption during the 2016 US elections (Guess, Nyhan, and Reifler, 2020) found that, in the pre-election period, unreliable websites accounted for only about 6% of the total news content consumed by Americans. If an intervention makes people skeptical of all news, the losses may outweigh the benefits.

Distrust of accurate information can be just as harmful as belief in falsehoods.

During a pandemic, this would mean distrusting both conspiracy theories about 5G and scientific evidence about vaccines.

Rising distrust benefits genuine manipulators.

When people trust no one — not the media, not science, not public institutions—they become vulnerable to actors who claim: “Trust only me, because I will reveal the WHOLE truth.”

focuses on identifying disinformation and pays little attention to accurate news. However, genuine skill in detecting fake news requires both. The cues the game emphasizes may not be unique to disinformation, as reputable newspapers also occasionally publish highly polarized content.

In other words, the so-called manipulation techniques taught by

are also used in legitimate journalism. Polarized content? Emotional language? These are attention-grabbing devices that outlets such as

The Guardian

The New York Times

, and other established publications use from time to time.

What do other studies say?

There was one exception: a 2023

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/acp.3995

by Ananya Iyengar and colleagues at St. Stephen's College in India found that, after playing Bad News, participants were better able to distinguish fake stories from factual information. This study was cited as evidence that inoculation interventions can be effective in non-Western contexts.

It was precisely this exception that Tina Seabrooke, together with Modirrousta-Galian and Higham, set out to examine in a new

https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-025-02827-x

conducted in 2026 with 150 participants in India. They addressed a key limitation of the original research by

balancing the stimuli

. Specifically, they used the same Indian news items, but half of the participants saw set A in the pre-test and set B in the post-test, while the other half saw the reverse.

The result?

The effect disappeared

. One set of news items was simply easier to classify than the other. The apparent “improvement” after playing Bad News was therefore due to participants encountering easier items in the post-test, rather than to any learning effect produced by the game.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-32962-1

by Robert McPhedran (2023, Scientific Reports, N = 2,430), conducted in a realistic social media environment, found that inoculation protects against engagement with disinformation more effectively than simple labeling of fake content.

The protection provided by inoculation was durable and did not depend on participants' level of cognitive reflection, unlike labeling

. To date, no published critiques or refutations of this study have appeared.

If not rational instruction, then what?

The evidence suggests that the problem may not lie in a lack of knowledge about manipulation techniques, but in the fact that

trying to protect one's identity overrides formal rules

When encountering a news story that affirms their group identity, evokes strong emotions, and reinforces their worldview, the brain will tend to accept it as true — regardless of whether they are familiar with the six DEPICT techniques.

Modirrousta-Galian, Higham, and Seabrooke

https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2023-50854-001

an alternative approach—

inductive learning

. Rather than studying rules and then applying them, individuals are presented with multiple examples and receive immediate feedback indicating the correct answer:

“Is this true or fake news?” → \[Answer\] → “Correct/Incorrect, here's why”

This approach is intended to develop intuitive understanding (tacit knowledge), rather than replace it with explicit knowledge. It does not require rote memorization of rules. Instead, it focuses on both components: recognizing fake news and recognizing accurate information.

Notably, the creators of

reached a similar conclusion independently. In refining the game, they

https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2025-10514-003.html

that feedback is a central component of effective learning. Results from six experiments were encouraging: feedback significantly improved discernment—the difference between average reliability ratings of accurate and fake news — with effect sizes (Cohen's d) ranging from 0.295 to 0.567, depending on the experiment.

However, when the same data were analyzed using ROC methods, the effects were substantially smaller: Cohen's d ranged from 0.06 to 0.19. This indicates that part of the improvement observed in average ratings reflected a shift in the trust threshold rather than a genuine improvement in discrimination. The extent of any remaining real effect remains an open question.

A lesson from cognitive warfare

The story of

is not merely the story of a single unsuccessful intervention. It illustrates a

fundamental mistake

in efforts to counter disinformation.

We tend to assume that the problem is a

lack of knowledge

“People do not understand manipulation techniques” → Teach them

“People do not know how to think critically” → Train them

“People do not understand how science works” → Explain it

However, research suggests that the problem lies in

rather than knowledge.

of recognizing fake news: tacit knowledge does operate. However, when a fake story reinforces their group identity, identity-protective cognition is activated—and suddenly all “six DEPICT techniques” are forgotten. As Julia Galef writes in

The Scout Mindset

, the difference between a soldier (who defends a position) and a scout (who seeks the truth) lies not in skills, but in

attempts to give soldiers better weapons. However, if the goal remains “protect my identity,” better weapons merely make them more effective soldiers—more skeptical of hostile messages, but also more skeptical of anything that threatens their worldview.

Real change

requires not better tools, but a different goal. Not “how to better recognize fake news about my group,” but “how to find the truth, even if I do not like it.” This, however, is far more difficult than playing a 15-minute game.

Key takeaway.

Psychological inoculation (“vaccination”) has shown that rational approaches can lose out to emotional and identity-based dynamics. When we attempt to “teach people to think correctly” without accounting for identity-protective cognition, the result is not improved discrimination, but generalized skepticism—which can be just as dangerous as gullibility.

A case relevant for Ukraine

In the fall of 2022, Google Jigsaw conducted a large-scale

https://medium.com/jigsaw/defanging-disinformations-threat-to-ukrainian-refugees-b164dbbc1c60

. Users in Czechia, Poland, and Slovakia were shown prebunking videos that deconstructed disinformation narratives about Ukrainian refugees and explained in advance how the manipulation worked. They were subsequently given surveys to determine whether their ability to recognize disinformation tactics had improved relative to a control group. Within the first two weeks, the campaign reached approximately one quarter of Poland's population and one third of the populations of Czechia and Slovakia. In total, the videos were viewed 38 million times—more than half the combined population of the three countries.

Google researchers found that those who watched the videos were better able to recognize manipulation techniques and were less likely to share fake news stories — the proportion of respondents who correctly identified manipulative tactics targeting refugees increased by 8%. However, the pattern varied across countries. The largest effect was observed in Poland. In Czechia, results were mixed — some test items showed improved recognition of manipulation after exposure to the videos, while others did not. Researchers suggest that, in some cases, this may have been related to the study design: certain items may have been too easy or too difficult, making changes in performance difficult to detect. In Slovakia, by contrast, the campaign produced no statistically significant effect — possibly because the Slovak-language videos were dubbed rather than explicitly produced for that market, as the researchers suggested.

https://www.brookings.edu/articles/preempting-putin-washingtons-campaign-of-intelligence-disclosures-is-complicating-moscows-plans-for-ukraine

illustrates the same principle: ahead of the full-scale invasion, the United States preemptively released intelligence about Russia's plans, including preparations for false-flag provocations. When the Kremlin later advanced these narratives, the audience had already been prepared. Although the primary aim of the British and US governments was to disrupt Russia's invasion plans, this effort also functioned as a classic prebunking intervention at the level of strategic communications.

Five shifts: from intuition to evidence-based practice

Practical recommendations based on research for those who work with information — journalists, analysts, educators, activists, and others — can be summarized as five shifts in approach.

From “you are wrong” to “someone is trying to deceive you”

Research consistently shows that when people are told they are mistaken, the brain shifts into a defensive mode. However, when they are told that someone is attempting to manipulate them, they are more likely to become allies of the person issuing the warning. Claude Steele's self-affirmation theory (1988)

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/bookseries/abs/pii/S0065260108602294

that people are far less defensive toward uncomfortable facts if they first have an opportunity to affirm their self-worth in another domain. In practice, this means that instead of writing “this is fake, and here is why you are wrong,” it is more effective to write “here is how this manipulation works, and here is who benefits from it.” Identify the beneficiary. People do not like being deceived — even when the deception is emotionally gratifying.

From refuting facts to motivating independent thinking

A single fake news story is a symptom. The manipulation technique is the disease. A person who has learned to recognize emotional framing, false dilemmas, and appeals to false authority and self-proclaimed “experts” is resilient to thousands of future fake news stories, not just the one debunked today. Research by Roozenbeek, Traberg, and van der Linden measured the inoculation effect in simple terms: after playing

, participants were more likely to identify disinformation correctly. The detection rate increased — meaning the intervention had worked. The logic was clear, and the result appeared convincing.

However, Modirrousta-Galian and Higham identified a fundamental limitation of this approach: it measured only part of the relevant outcome. When researchers revisited data from earlier inoculation studies, the conclusion was different: inoculation did not improve the ability to discriminate disinformation; it merely shifted the trust threshold. In other words,

did not teach people to think better, but to doubt more. This does not mean that inoculation as an approach has definitively failed — subsequent meta-analyses with broader samples provide a more nuanced picture. However, the shift they introduced is fundamental: they reframed the question from “do people recognize more fake news?” to “do people become better at distinguishing truth from falsehood?” These are fundamentally different questions.

At the same time, the problem of trust in disinformation often lies not in a lack of knowledge, but in motivation. Therefore, training in manipulation techniques should be complemented by materials that explain how our own thinking works, including confirmation bias and the difference between “defending my position” and “seeking the truth.” The goal is for people to understand why they believe what they believe — not simply to believe less.

From a binary verdict to open uncertainty

“True/false” is a convenient format, but the world is rarely binary. Tetlock's research on superforecasters (2015)

https://sobrief.com/uk/books/superforecasting

that people who think in probabilistic terms make significantly more accurate forecasts.

https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1913678117

by Annemarie van der Bles et al. (2020) on trust in experts further suggests that, despite common concerns, transparent communication of uncertainty generally does not undermine trust (although this question requires further study, as empirical evidence on the subject remains limited).

The Scout Mindset

(2021), Julia Galef

https://ftp.spadok.org.ua/ord/myslennya-rozvidnyka-yak-prypynyty-obmanyuvaty-sebe-j-pobachyty-najkrasche-rishennya.pdf

the distinction between “uncertainty about oneself” (which reduces trust) and “uncertainty about the world” (which signals intellectual honesty). In practice, stating that “based on the available evidence, this claim is highly likely to be false, but we will continue to monitor the situation” is a stronger position than issuing a categorical “FAKE,” which may later require correction.

From infallibility to a culture of updates

Brendan Nyhan (2021,

https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117

one reason corrections do not work at the societal level: their effects fade rapidly. This means that countering disinformation requires not one-off publications, but a systematic, ongoing effort. It also requires honesty: organizations that publish corrections openly and regularly build trust more effectively than those that seek to appear infallible.

In practice, the formulation should not be “we made a mistake,” but “we have updated our conclusion based on the latest available information.”

From one-size-fits-all to strategic diagnosis

Not all fake news stories are the same. A false factual claim (for example, an incorrect statistic) is amenable to standard correction. However, a belief that has become part of a person's identity (for example, views on vaccines, language, or geopolitical alignment) is not. Identity-based beliefs have recognizable markers: when a person says “I am \[X\]” rather than “I think \[X\],” any criticism is perceived as a personal attack, and no factual evidence is sufficient to dislodge that position.

Allocating the same resources to both types is inefficient. Identity-based topics require different tools: prebunking, training in recognizing manipulative techniques, and long-term media literacy strategies, rather than one-off fact-checks.

What does the wartime context change?

Ukraine, which has been at war with Russia since 2014 and has been engaged in a full-scale defensive war since February 2022, has become one of the most important testing grounds for research on countering disinformation. Most of the studies discussed above were conducted in peaceful democratic contexts. Ukraine operates in a different reality, and this distinction must be taken into account.

In a large-scale

https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0307090

, Ethan Porter et al. (2024,

) conducted simultaneous experiments in five countries: Belarus, Estonia, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Ukraine. One group of participants was shown fact-checks debunking Russian fake news about the war in Ukraine, while another group was not. Participants were then asked how strongly they believed the false claim and what their views were on Russia's war against Ukraine. The results are clear: fact-checking pro-Kremlin disinformation reduces belief in specific false claims.

However, it does not change attitudes toward which side to support in the war. Fact-checking works — but not necessarily in the way one might expect

“The other side” may itself be an active adversary

. In a peaceful context, the recommendation to “listen to the other side” refers to overcoming one's own echo chamber. In wartime, however, “the other side” is often a state propaganda apparatus with multibillion-dollar budgets. The objective is not to “find a kernel of truth” in the Kremlin's position, but to understand the mechanisms of its manipulation to counter them effectively.

Stress degrades cognitive functioning

. Combat stress, PTSD, and anxiety caused by shelling significantly impair the ability to think critically. An audience living under missile attacks differs cognitively from one not living in war and not directly experiencing its consequences. Journalists and analysts working with wartime content likewise require psychological support, not only professional development.

Building institutions in advance is essential

. RAND's conclusion (2024) has implications far beyond Ukraine: countries seeking resilience against disinformation during crises must build the necessary institutions in peacetime. Fact-checking infrastructure, media literacy networks, and coordination between the state and civil society are not luxuries, but strategic assets.

Instead of a conclusion: cognitive sovereignty

The MIT study showed that falsehood

spreads faster

https://ide.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/2017-IDE-Research-Brief-False-News.pdf

than truth because it is more emotionally compelling. Kahan's research showed that people with high analytical ability

can be just as vulnerable

https://rcgd.isr.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/motivated\_numeracy\_and\_enlightened\_selfgovernment.pdf

to identity-based fake news as others. Porter et al. (2024) showed, across five countries, that it is possible to change a specific belief

without changing identity

https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0307090

. Research from Cambridge showed that it is possible to

”inoculate” people against manipulations

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-019-0279-9

before they occur.

All these findings form a coherent picture. Countering disinformation is not merely a matter of fact-checking. It involves engaging with human psychology — with motivation, identity, attention, and trust. It is a field in which science already offers answers, but practice has yet to fully incorporate them.

For Ukraine, which for more than ten years has been confronting one of the world's largest disinformation machines—and since February 2022 has been waging a full-scale defensive war—this struggle is not abstract. Every debunked fake news story, every person “inoculated” against manipulation, and every organization that preserves trust through honesty represents a building block in defending what may be called the nation's cognitive sovereignty.

Protecting it is no less important than defending physical borders.
